author: The Elephant
title: Alternative Leadership As A Decolonial Paradigm
content:
Sarova Stanley, Nairobi | 11 November 2026




Theme: Reimagining Leadership, Reclaiming Citizen Agency




Dr. Kawive Wambua;




The leadership and team of Inuka Kenya Ni Sisi!;

Representatives of civil society;

Distinguished guests;

Fellow Kenyans:




Good morning.




Thank you for inviting me to join you at the launch of the Inuka! Angaza Kura Campaign.




Your theme, “Reimagining Leadership, Reclaiming Citizen Agency,” brings us to the central question of our democracy: The Constitution proclaims Sovereignty of the people, but who truly exercises power in Kenya?




Is it the citizen whose taxes sustain the state, whose labour builds the economy, and whose vote confers authority? Or is it the officeholder who, once elected, hijacks power and behaves like the master, relegating citizens to subjects?




What must the citizens do to reclaim their agency, their power? 




You have asked me to reflect on “Alternative Leadership as a Decolonial Paradigm.”




The language may sound academic, but the issue is profoundly practical.




It concerns the relationship between a Kenyan citizen and the person entrusted to serve them. It concerns whether a police officer offers protection or inspires fear; whether a public office provides a service or demands a favour; whether public money builds opportunity or finances private privilege.




Above all, it concerns whether independence has become an everyday experience of dignity and quality services for us. 




From subjects to citizens




The colonial state was organised to control people and extract resources. Its authority flowed downwards. The population was expected to comply, while those who governed were insulated from meaningful accountability to the governed.




Independence was supposed to transform that relationship.




Yet changing the nationality of those occupying public office could not, by itself, dismantle the habits, incentives and institutions of domination, without changing the mindset of the office holders. Understanding leadership to be service and sacrifice, rather than entitlement and a life of privilege at the expense of basic needs for the people. Imagining leadership as an opportunity to ensure protection of the rights of the people and to uphold and affirm the dignity of the people you serve. Ensuring that, as a leader, you remain loyal to the purpose- service with openness and accountability. These are the minimum standards demanded by the constitution we gifted ourselves. 




Whenever leadership demands obedience without accountability, the colonial model or inheritance survives. Whenever citizens must seek political patronage to obtain public services, it survives. Whenever criticism is treated as disloyalty, it survives.




Decolonising leadership therefore requires us to confront the exercise of power in our own time.




We must ask whether the state serves citizens as people with rights, or manages them as subjects who should remain grateful for favours.




A hospital is a public responsibility. A road is a public investment. Education is an investment in the nation’s future. Every service by leaders is part of their duty to us, funded by our taxes, not a favour. 




None of these should become a personal gift for which citizens owe a politician their silence. Service should not be in exchange for citizens losing their freedom to exercise their right to demand accountability. Service must never be at the cost of citizens losing their agency, their power to oversee leaders, the government. 




An alternative must be radically different in word and deed. 




Comrades,




The word “alternative” carries an obligation.




Those of us who seek to offer alternative leadership must demonstrate how we would govern differently. We must affirm our allegiance to the Constitution, whose main objective is to restrain, or in other words, limit the exercise of power.  Alternative leadership must affirm citizens’ right to seek accountability and readiness to vacate office should citizens unequivocally so demand. The Alternative leadership must pledge allegiance to the Constitution and the people of Kenya, and affirm the sovereignty of the people. Demonstrate an understanding that leadership is a privilege to serve, not a title deed to rule over the people. Our utterances and actions as alternative leadership must so demonstrate. 




It is insufficient to condemn arrogance in government while practising it within our political parties. We cannot promise inclusion while silencing young people and women in our own organisations. We cannot demand transparency from others while avoiding scrutiny ourselves.




Our credibility begins with our conduct.




An alternative worthy of public trust must be rule-based, and must make room for disagreement. It must select leaders through fair processes, disclose conflicts of interest, reject political violence, and accept that public office is a temporary responsibility.




This includes me and all my colleagues.  I believe this is our obligation, as people offering an alternative, rather than more of the same. 




I have offered myself for the presidency in the 2027 General Election because I believe Kenya deserves an alternative. An alternative grounded in constitutionalism, integrity, economic justice, and respect for the sovereignty of the people. I believe we can build a government that treats public resources as a trust, not a source of private enrichment; an economy that rewards hard work and creates opportunity; and institutions that serve citizens rather than those who happen to occupy positions of power.




Citizens should scrutinise my record, question my proposals and hold me to the standards I ask of others. No leader should seek exemption from accountability because of past service, personal sacrifice or political popularity.




This is the alternative I offer to Kenyans. But let me also say that the transformation of a nation cannot be the work of one individual. No president, however capable, can substitute for strong institutions, active citizens, and a society that demands accountability. That is why we should be individually and collectively intentional,  as we elect all six leaders on the ballot, not just the president. 




Reclaiming the citizen’s voice




This is why the Inuka! Angaza Kura Campaign matters.




By inviting Kenyans to define the leadership values they expect, identify potential leaders, and share electoral experiences, this initiative can help reverse a familiar political habit: politicians prescribing the choices while citizens are asked only to applaud.




The conversation should begin with the citizen.




What does a mother seeking treatment for her child expect from government? What does a graduate searching for work need from the economy? What does a farmer require to earn a fair return? What would make a person living with a disability an equal participant in public life?




Citizens’ experiences must shape our political priorities.




Citizen agency means having the knowledge, confidence, organisation and freedom to influence decisions. It extends beyond voting day into public budgeting, community organising, oversight and the daily demand for fair treatment.




A citizen who asks how money was spent is exercising responsibility. A journalist investigating wrongdoing is performing a public service. A young person questioning authority deserves an answer. A citizen scrutinizing the record of aspiring leaders, including incumbents who put themselves forward for re-election, is exercising responsibility, and sovereignty as the employer for the journalist b being sought. 




Leadership should welcome that scrutiny.




Dignity must govern the use of power




A different political culture must begin with respect for human life and dignity. 




No administration should treat abduction, torture or unlawful killing as instruments of governance. No family should have to search for a loved one while public institutions evade responsibility.




Security must mean that people are safe, including when they disagree with those in power.




Likewise, accountability must reach those who command institutions, authorise expenditure and make decisions. It cannot end with the most junior officer while the powerful remain beyond examination.




We must build a culture in which evidence matters, investigations are credible, and justice is pursued without political favour or revenge.




The same principle applies to public resources.




Every diverted shilling has a human consequence: medicine unavailable, a classroom unfinished, a supplier unpaid, an opportunity lost.




Alternative leadership must make public expenditure understandable and open to scrutiny. Citizens should be able to establish what was purchased, what it cost, who supplied it and whether it was delivered.




Economic freedom and freedom of thought




Political freedom becomes fragile when poverty leaves citizens vulnerable to coercion.




When access to work, relief or opportunity depends on political loyalty, hardship becomes a means of control.




Our responsibility is to expand people’s independence through education, productive work, accessible services and fair economic opportunity, as well as continuous civic engagement.




We must free political debate from the assumption that ethnicity determines judgment.




Our communities give us identity, belonging and cultural richness. But no politician owns a community’s conscience. No Kenyan should be instructed to excuse misconduct because the person responsible speaks their language.




We can cherish our identities while demanding the same standards of every leader.




Turning participation into lasting power




As this campaign develops, I encourage you to connect digital participation with community engagement.




Reach citizens who lack smartphones or reliable internet. Use accessible formats and languages people understand. Protect participants’ personal information. Make space for disagreement, and establish fair ways to assess the information people submit.




Above all, show citizens what happens after they contribute.




Participation loses meaning when people speak, and nothing responds. Its value grows when their concerns become public questions, their proposals shape commitments, and those commitments can be tracked.




Let this platform help citizens ask every aspiring leader:




What have you done? What are you proposing? How will it be financed? How will we measure delivery? And how will you answer for failure?




These questions should follow us beyond the campaign platform and into office.




The republic we must build




Fellow Kenyans,




The biggest change we seek is a relationship in which public power recognises its limits and citizens recognise their strength.




We should judge leadership by whether institutions work fairly even when the leader is absent; whether services reach people without political intervention; and whether citizens can challenge authority without fear.




That is the promise we must make real.




Let us build a Kenya in which dignity requires no connection, opportunity requires no patron, and justice requires no permission from the powerful.




As we launch the Inuka! Angaza Kura Campaign, let us commit to an active, informed and organised citizenry that can choose leaders wisely and hold them accountable consistently.




Inuka, Kenya. Ask the difficult questions. Examine the answers. Organise peacefully. Participate fully.




The republic belongs to its people, and its leadership must always answer to them.




Thank you.

author: Nelly Madegwa
title: Pregnancy in a Warming Africa
content:
At 8:30 a.m., Stella is usually already at the Kakamega Forest dispensary in Kakamega County, western Kenya, for her antenatal care (ANC) appointment. Seven months pregnant, she has learnt to organise her household around the rising heat, doing most of her chores when temperatures are lower.




The clinic is 2.5 kilometres away, a distance she walks. Arriving early allows her to complete her check-ups and begin the journey home before the sun becomes unbearable.




Her routine reflects a change that Doreen Atamba, a community health promoter who has supported expectant mothers for the past ten years, has observed among women attending the facility. Increasingly, expectant mothers arrive between 8 a.m. and 10 a.m., with fewer coming after 10 a.m. By late morning, attendance drops considerably.




Atamba says the heat is affecting not only when women seek antenatal care but also their comfort and well-being at home. Some expectant mothers complain that intense temperatures make everyday activities difficult and disrupt their sleep.




“Some of them tell me they are really struggling with the heat, even at night when they are trying to sleep,” she says.




To help them cope, Atamba encourages pregnant women to wear loose-fitting clothing, drink plenty of water, avoid unnecessary exposure to extreme heat, rest frequently and seek relief in cooler places, especially shaded areas.




These everyday adjustments are taking place amid rising temperatures and growing concern about the effects of climate change on maternal and newborn health.




Across Africa, experts in Kenya, South Africa, Senegal and Nigeria are increasingly concerned about how climate-related extremes are affecting pregnant women and newborns. Extreme heat can cause dehydration and physical strain, while drought, flooding, food insecurity and disrupted healthcare services can compound the risks. Experts say the consequences depend not only on the weather but also on women’s living and working conditions, access to water and nutrition, and the ability of health facilities to provide safe care.




Heat and pregnancy




Pregnancy places additional demands on the body. During extreme heat, dehydration and the effort required to regulate body temperature can put additional strain on the heart and circulatory system. Researchers are still investigating how this stress may affect the placenta and developing baby.




Ijeoma Solarin, a senior researcher at Wits Planetary Health Research, and Kimberly McAlpine, a medical student and PhD researcher at Wits University, point to growing evidence associating high temperatures with preterm birth, stillbirth, low birth weight and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.




A 2025 

study

 by Carrie Ngongo and colleagues, analysing 22.7 million births in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, found that each 1°C increase in temperature above 34°C was associated with an additional 2.3 stillbirths per 1,000 births and 27.3 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.




A separate 

study

 at a Johannesburg hospital linked high temperatures early in pregnancy to approximately 1.8 times the risk of severe hypertensive disorders, including pre-eclampsia and eclampsia.




Research

 involving pregnant subsistence farmers in The Gambia has also documented signs of fetal distress during hot weather, including unusual changes in the baby’s heart rate and increased resistance to blood flow through the umbilical cord, which supplies oxygen and nutrients from the placenta.




The scale of concern extends beyond individual studies. A 

Wellcome-commissioned poll

 of 1,001 healthcare professionals in Australia, Brazil, India, the United Kingdom and Zimbabwe found that 98 per cent had cared for a pregnant woman whose health they believed had been adversely affected by extreme heat. Meanwhile, 99 per cent reported caring for a baby whose health they believed had been adversely affected by extreme heat.




These findings reflect healthcare professionals’ reported experiences and perceptions, rather than estimates of the proportion of pregnant women or babies experiencing medically confirmed heat-related harm. Nevertheless, they highlight concerns among health workers about the effects of extreme heat on mothers and babies.




As climate change drives more frequent and intense heat extremes, exposure to dangerous temperatures is becoming an increasing health risk. However, this risk is not experienced equally. Social and economic inequalities mean some women have fewer resources and less ability to protect themselves.




For Solarin and McAlpine, the risks cannot be separated from the conditions in which women live.




“Heat exposure is shaped as much by social conditions as by the weather,” they explain.




In informal settlements, corrugated-metal homes can trap heat indoors, while unreliable electricity makes fans difficult to use and water shortages limit opportunities to cool down and stay hydrated. Women who farm, trade outdoors, cook in hot environments or collect water may also have little control over how long they spend in the heat.




Poor sleeping conditions can compound the problem, leaving women exhausted and with little relief even at night.




“The evidence points to the same conclusion across settings that climate exposures amplify existing inequalities rather than creating new ones,” Solarin and McAlpine say.




When avoiding heat is not an option




Climate scientist Dr Jeanne Sambou says pregnancy places additional physiological demands on the body, while many women have limited control over their exposure to heat. A pregnant woman may still need to work outdoors, sell goods at a market, process fish, cook in a hot environment or travel considerable distances to obtain healthcare.




Sambou also emphasises the importance of humidity. When temperatures and humidity are both high, the body has greater difficulty cooling itself through sweating.




Climate Central’s 2026 

analysis

 found that the global average number of days with dangerous humid heat more than doubled, from 10 days a year in the 1970s to 23 days between 2016 and 2025. The analysis identified human-induced climate change as the main driver of this increase.




The Climate Shift Index 

interactive tool

 offers a way to explore this influence locally. In Kakamega, western Kenya, the tool showed that climate change made a forecast daily maximum wet-bulb temperature of 19.3°C on 28 October at least 60 times more likely.




Wet-bulb temperature combines heat and humidity to indicate how effectively the body can cool itself. The reading was below Climate Central’s 25°C threshold for dangerous humid heat, but illustrates why assessing heat risks requires looking beyond air temperature alone.




Two women exposed to the same outdoor temperature may face different levels of risk depending on their work, housing, health status and access to cooling and healthcare. Advising women simply to avoid the heat may accomplish little if their livelihoods and household responsibilities leave them with few alternatives.




In Kenya, Chris Abuor, executive director of Kuza Trust, a policy and narrative change organisation working on community-led public health and climate resilience, describes extreme heat as an overlooked threat in rural communities and informal settlements.




“Extreme heat is a silent crisis that I think, as civil society and communities, we have not really wrapped our heads around,” he says.




Abuor points to pregnant women working on farms and those living in poorly ventilated iron-sheet structures in informal settlements. In communities experiencing water shortages, women may also have to walk long distances to collect water, increasing their exposure to heat and physical exertion.




Thandi, who lives in Alexandra, Johannesburg, illustrates the difficulty of following heat-health advice when resources are limited. During her first pregnancy, she did not realise that her exhaustion, difficulty sleeping and discomfort in the heat were worth raising with a healthcare professional.




“Because it was my first pregnancy, I thought feeling exhausted, struggling to sleep and finding the heat difficult to cope with were normal parts of pregnancy. During a clinic visit, I mentioned these difficulties to the clinician and was advised to use a portable fan. However, with the cost of electricity and frequent power cuts, I could not always rely on one,” she says.




Her experience highlights the need for heat-health advice to take account of the practical constraints women face in accessing reliable and affordable cooling.




Drawing on his experience in Kitere Village in Rongo Sub-County, Abuor describes a stream that dried up following a prolonged drought. Women who traditionally bear responsibility for fetching household water must then travel farther to obtain it.




Such experiences reflect a wider challenge across the Horn of Africa, where a 

study

 found that human-induced climate change intensified the 2020–2023 drought by increasing temperatures and worsening the effects of low rainfall.




The problem extends to health facilities. Where maternity services lack a constant water supply because of drought, maintaining hygiene during delivery becomes more difficult, potentially increasing the risk of infection after childbirth.




In Nigeria, Dr H.M., a paediatrician and public-health specialist, says heat stress is among a wider range of climate-related risks that can affect maternal and newborn health. She says newborns deserve particular attention because their ability to regulate body temperature is still developing.




“One area receiving too little attention is the effect of climate change on newborns and the very early stages of life,” she says.




What researchers still need to understand




Despite growing international evidence linking extreme heat with adverse pregnancy outcomes, important gaps remain in understanding how these relationships vary across African settings.




Dr Sambou points to a Senegalese study covering more than two million births between 2018 and 2022, which found no statistically significant association between average monthly temperatures and stillbirth or maternal mortality.




She cautions against interpreting this as evidence that heat poses no risk. Monthly averages can conceal short periods of intense heat, while limitations in health and exposure data make it difficult to establish the full relationship.




Temperature recorded at a weather station may not reflect the conditions a woman experiences inside her home, at work or while travelling to a clinic. The intensity, duration and timing of heat exposure may also influence the risks.




Solarin and McAlpine identify another important gap: understanding the biological pathways through which heat affects pregnancy and determining which interventions can prevent harm.




At Wits Planetary Health Research, the Bio-HEAT study is investigating the biological pathways linking heat exposure to preterm birth and other adverse maternal and child health outcomes in South Africa.




In Senegal, SPRINT-Sen examines extreme heat alongside breastfeeding and maternal mental health in northern Senegal.




Both initiatives address questions that extend beyond whether a risk exists to how it develops and what can be done to reduce it.




“We already know enough about heat risk in pregnancy to act now,” Solarin and McAlpine say, while arguing that further African research is needed to identify effective interventions and inform investment.




Policies exist, but implementation remains a challenge




South Africa has a National Climate Change Adaptation Strategy, National Heat Health Action Guidelines and an impact-based warning system operated by the South African Weather Service. Pregnant women are also identified as a vulnerable population in national heat-health guidance.




Yet Solarin and McAlpine describe the gap between policy recognition and practical implementation as substantial.




“The gap is between naming these risks in planning strategies and guidelines, and actually operationalising that recognition and seeing action on the ground,” they explain.




They identify five priority areas: public awareness, clinical protocols, health-facility preparedness, healthcare-worker training and better data.




When a heat warning is issued, clinics need clear guidance on what to do differently, which women may require closer follow-up and what advice healthcare workers should provide. Health workers also need training to recognise heat as a potential risk during pregnancy.




Facilities require adequate ventilation, shaded waiting areas, reliable drinking water and contingency plans for power outages and water shortages.




Temperature-sensitive medicines present another concern. Solarin and McAlpine highlight the need to protect the storage conditions of oxytocin, which is used to prevent and treat postpartum haemorrhage. Prolonged exposure to inappropriate temperatures can compromise medicine quality.




Better data is also essential. Without routinely recording heat exposure alongside maternal health information, it is difficult to monitor impacts or evaluate whether interventions are effective.




At the launch of a new global framework in October this year, the World Health Organization (WHO), alongside the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), UNICEF and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), highlighted the need to improve monitoring of heat exposure and its effects on pregnant women, newborns and children. The framework proposes priority indicators to help countries track health risks, strengthen preparedness and guide targeted interventions.




In Kenya, Abuor argues that the principal challenge is not a lack of policy recognition but a failure to turn commitments into action.




He says climate-resilient infrastructure and resources must reach primary-care dispensaries and rural maternity facilities, rather than being concentrated at major county referral hospitals.




Abuor also advocates stronger supply-chain monitoring to ensure essential medical supplies and emergency obstetric kits are available at frontline facilities, including during floods that disrupt transport routes.




Through Kuza Trust and the Resilience Action Network Africa civil society working group, he says they are working to strengthen community capacity, improve public health surveillance and enhance counties’ ability to respond to climate-related health risks, including extreme heat.




Abuor says the work also draws on broader public-health preparedness approaches, including the 7-1-7 framework for improving the detection and response to infectious disease outbreaks.




In Nigeria, Dr H.M. emphasises the need for climate-resilient facilities and continuity plans for antenatal, delivery and postnatal services. She recommends strengthening community health workers, mobile outreach services, referral systems and emergency transportation so that care can continue when women cannot reach health facilities.




“Implementation should move beyond having a policy document to actually changing how health services prepare for climate risks,” she says.




Turning warnings into protection




Across the four countries, experts point to practical measures that could help protect pregnant women and newborns from extreme heat and other climate-related risks.




Solarin and McAlpine recommend affordable interventions such as reflective roofs, window shading, improved cross-ventilation and shaded waiting areas. Health facilities also need reliable drinking water and contingency plans to maintain essential services during power outages and water shortages.




Heat warnings should prompt specific action, not simply alert the public to rising temperatures. Antenatal clinics could use existing communication channels to share practical advice, while healthcare workers identify women who may need additional support.




Community engagement is equally important. The experts point to work in Kilifi County, Kenya, involving spouses, mothers-in-law and community leaders in discussions about sharing domestic responsibilities and shifting strenuous activities to cooler hours. The approach recognises that women may have limited control over their workloads and need support from their households and communities.




Dr Sambou advocates integrating heat-related advice into routine antenatal care, including guidance on hydration, reducing heat exposure where possible, recognising warning signs and knowing when to seek medical attention. She also stresses the need to prepare for drought and flooding, which can undermine nutrition, livelihoods and access to healthcare.




For Abuor, stronger links between meteorological services, health information systems and frontline health workers are essential to ensure that climate warnings lead to timely responses. Dr H.M. similarly calls for climate adaptation to be integrated into existing maternal, newborn and child health programmes, supported by resilient facilities and plans to maintain care during disruptions.




But adaptation, while essential, cannot eliminate the growing risks if global temperatures continue to rise. The underlying cause is greenhouse gas emissions, particularly from burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas, as well as activities including deforestation and industrial agriculture.




Without decisive action to reduce these emissions, extreme heat will continue to intensify, placing additional pressure on pregnant women, newborns and already overstretched health services.




With COP31 kicking off yesterday, protecting maternal and newborn health must be part of the wider climate response. This requires both adaptation measures, such as climate-resilient health facilities, and decisive action to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Accelerating the transition to renewable energy and ensuring that lower-income countries have the resources to protect their populations will be essential.




Ultimately, protecting mothers and babies will require more than advice on coping with hot weather. It will depend on whether health services, communities and policymakers can turn growing evidence of climate-related risks into practical support for women throughout pregnancy and childbirth, while also tackling the emissions that are making extreme heat more dangerous.




As Dr Sambou puts it, “The question is no longer only whether pregnant women are vulnerable. It is what we do differently because they are.”

author: Trevor Ngwane
title: African Labour and Liberation
content:
African Labour and Liberation

 brings together the experiences of workers, trade unions and labour movements across the continent to ask what they can tell us about work, power and liberation today. We assembled this collection because of the surprisingly few recent accounts of the emergence of a class politics on the continent. Labour is central to understanding the present political economy of Africa.  More than 90 percent of Africa’s 500 million workers work in informal and precarious jobs in a labour force that will grow rapidly in the next three decades.




The social and political mobilization of workers in multifarious contexts across the continent is imperative to improving their socio-economic conditions. It is necessary to situate Africa’s workers at the centre. This collection starts from the premise that labour struggles are essential to improving the conditions of work and stamping out poverty and inequality that confront most African workers today and form the basis for building new forms of collective power.




This heterodox collec­tion finds six primary patterns prevalent in the struggle for working-class liberation in the post-independence era.




1. Most governments in Africa are comprador-bureaucratic regimes beholden to foreign capital and imperialists’ interests to protect and maintain unequal exchange of trade and the attenuation of demands by the masses for national control over natural resources and production. Comprador-bureaucratic regimes remain loyal to their post-colonial powers and pay fleeting attention to national sustainability, the rights of women, natu­ral ecology, and the ever-growing needs of the masses for health care, education, housing, infrastructure, water, and electricity.




Government legislation to defend popular interests that have been enacted by national assemblies are rarely fully implemented and are likely to be opposed by international banks and lenders, predominantly from the West through structural adjustment programs that undermine evanescent attempts to ameliorate the most significant challenges.




2. Diverse workers’ movements form to resist t the comprador-bureaucratic political economies which formed in the colonial era which most often extract surplus value from workers and natural resources from the continent  through what  Arghiri Emmanuel  identified as 

unequal exchange of trade

, and despoiling, and plundering African nations. Control is maintained by local elites attached to state power who are beneficiaries of rentier capitalism. These national elites have welcomed Western powers to establish military bases osten­sibly to establish peace and order.




In most instances, the emergence of violence and disorder were generated by Western military intervention. However, as Samir Amin shows, workers and peasants drive the enduring imperative for the formation of national projects for popular sovereignty, which are often imperfect and challenged by imperialists seeking to maintain the unequal exchange of trade.




3. African states are ruled by comprador state-centric bureaucratic elites who maintain rentier capitalism as the primary source of revenue rather than investing in productive technology. The historical pattern is opposition to the redistribution of wealth and income to the masses.




This process, in which bureaucratic elements seek to transform themselves – sometimes successful sometimes not, but nearly always drawing links to imperial­ism and thereby fusing the bureaucratic and comprador elements – can be seen nearly everywhere. Unquestionably, compliant and often corrupt political elites provide the patina of legitimacy for all practical purposes, for the expansion of inequality.




4. In Africa, racial justice must include an anti-imperialist per­spective which acknowledges the legacy of European colonialism and the protracted nature of imperialism which sustains racial subordina­tion. Markedly, South Africa, a semi-peripheral mineral-rich state, did not redistribute wealth and property with the end of political apartheid and the development of a superficially democratic state. Black South Africans, composing over 80 percent of the country’s 65 million popu­lation, remain marginalized through the 1994 accords, which did not include a redistribution of wealth and resources – causing higher levels of poverty and inequality and impeding the working class from improv­ing its living standards.




5. Women constitute a large proportion of the African labour force, while also being disproportionately concentrated in precarious and insecure forms of work. Their labour is central to the reproduction of the economy, both through their participation in vital productive sectors and through forms of unpaid and underpaid labour that sustain households and communities.




Two women selling okpa at the Eke Awka Market in Awka, Anambra State, Nigeria (Wikimedia Commons, 2026)




This is particularly significant on a continent where, despite rapid urbanisation, more than half of the population continues to live in rural areas. Women are central to subsistence production and food sovereignty, while their role as primary caregivers places them at the centre of social reproduction. Any account of labour and liberation must therefore attend not only to women’s position within waged employment, but also to the often invisible labour through which they reproduce life, sustain communities and secure livelihoods.




6. The rural and urban economy, which is dominated by precarious employment, is also produced and amplified by climate uncertainty primarily instigated by Western consumption. A formula for social justice must include eco-socialist perspectives, ecological concerns and the extent to which these have been and are addressed by African labour movements. We attach importance to trade unions as sites of radical democracy and decolonial politics.




However, there is also significant invention and development that has taken place within African trade unions in different times and places that must be accentuated. We believe that trade unions and working-class organisa­tions must be tested, from case to case, rather than asserted, because of the proliferation of African trade unions which have developed forms of organisations and struggle that are necessary, novel, innovative and effective.




Taken together, enduring patterns of labour resistance demonstrate the enduring centrality of workers and popular movements to struggles for political and economic transformation and anti-imperialism. The histories gathered in 

African Labour and Liberation

 show that labour is not only understood simply through the workplace or trade union but must be situated within the anti-imperialist contestation over natural resources and the unceasing struggle to achieve, genuine popular sovereignty.




Concomitantly, these histories reveal that existing workers’ organisations on the continent are not uniform or even the vehicle for advancing the interests of the masses who are living under informal and precarious conditions. Across contexts, workers and their class allies have developed distinct modes of organising, resisting and building collective power.




African Labour and Liberation

 foregrounds histories of differentiated movements that resist enduring forms of domination and lay the groundwork for new terrains of conflict in opposition to internal oppression and imperialist domination. Far from being peripheral to the history of labour, they are central to understanding how working people have confronted exploitation and sought to reshape the societies in which they live.

title: Book Review: From Mau Mau to Ruto-Must-Go: A Scrapbook of Essays on Kenya’s Struggle Against Imperialism
content:
I recently read a review of the book, 

From MAU MAU to RUTO-MUST-GO: A Scrapbook of Essays on Kenya’s Struggle Against Imperialism,

 

by Teddy Odira, a young lawyer in Nairobi who published in The Platform for Law, Justice, and Society. I shared the review with one of the co-editors of the book, Shiraz Durrani, and asked him what he thought. This is was his response via a WhatsApp text:




It’s a brilliant review, I think. He understands the undercurrents that the book explores and identifies key issues, like land, that have driven resistance. He also sees resistance as an on-going, incomplete struggle. Very well done!




What is well said by another is mine. In this review, I want to glorify the work of the artist movements in Kenya for breathing life into the Constitution of Kenya, 2010, particularly 

Article 33

 that decrees freedom of expression. This freedom of expression has limitations. It is the freedom of artistic creativity that is glorified in two of the articles in the book. They glorify cartoonists and Social Justice Theatre (SJCCTT). Freedom of artistic creativity in Kenya is valued by others, including the two mentioned. The others include: poets, spoken word artists, graffiti artists, songwriters, singers, comedians, filmmakers, and others. Freedom of artistic creativity has been a radical site of struggle in the implementation of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010. Freedom of expression under the Constitution has been the subject of a recently published scholarly work.




This Constitution has been described as progressive and transformative because of the process of its making, its texts on objectives, purpose, and vision to reform, by non-reformist reforms, which maintain the status quo in Kenya. While the ruling elite find the Constitution inconvenient and abstract, these sites of struggle have used provisions of the Constitution to craft political demands, breathe life into these sites through uprising, robust public participation, mass action, and public interest litigation. The quest for an authentic patriotic alternative political leadership is a continuous struggle anchored in these constitutional sites of struggle that the ruling elite has refused to implement. It is argued that such an alternative political leadership that is authentic and patriotic will implement the Constitution by consolidating gains made, and rescuing the weaknesses that are encountered during the process of its implementation.




Glorification




A: In Praise of Cartoonists: Ruo Kimani-Ruo




Ruo Kimani-Ruo praises the cartoonists in words that should not be paraphrased:







…, 

there has emerged an unprecedented form of political cartoons artwork which has been launched in Kenya with sizzling, scorching, blistering cartoon editorials and other graphics and caricatures of public figures that express the artists’ opinions, with celebrated cartoon artists Celeste and Maddo

 

being joined by Yoko and others-all freely and fearlessly expressing their opinions on public issues and the individuals in government and thereby shedding light on the public mood on issues.…










With these political cartoons, the artists have had a field day and typically combined artistic skills, hyperbole and satire to question authority. The cartoons have drawn attention to, among other things, corruption, electoral inequalities, political abductions and other social ills including violence- and the Consolidated Fund at Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) where billions of shillings are being ‘siphoned and stashed in offshore accounts in the West; and suspicions of embezzlement.







The genius of the cartoonists that I have encountered over decades lies in the interpretation of their work for the powers that be, and the citizens themselves. They are always armed with many interpretations of their cartoons. They use those interpretations to either stay safe when confronted by elites and their machinery of violence, or to mobilize the citizens around the key messages. They invariably keep their mouths shut and let their work engage both the enemy and the friend. Their work requires great critical thinking, taking ideological and political positions in breathing life into the provisions of the Constitution to energize non-reformist reforms.




B: In Praise of Theatre Artists:

 

Zachary J Patterson




Zachary J Pattern glorifies the Social Justice Centres Travelling Theatre (SJCTT) in the following paragraphs:







Interactive scenes show an all-too familiar tale of the oppressed and their oppressors-the spectators become ‘spect-actors’. It is a brilliant way of renewing hope, inspiring the imagination and reviving resistance

…. 










Inspired by communist playwright Bertolt Brecht’s notion of art as tool that can help shape our social conditions, members of SJCTT approach their performance as active participants of the class struggle. The provocative thespians of SJCTT use common language rooted in local knowledge to cut through the apolitical noise and disrupt the established order, exhibiting a clear political perspective drawn from Marxist political theory. Shaped by their surrounding social conditions and informed by historical and contemporary realities, SJCTT deploys techniques of Augusto Boal’s Theatre of the Oppressed to analyze social problems and address the factors of the oppression.










…Their performances are shaped both by appreciation for Kenya’s history of resistance and their shared experiences, resulting in programs rich with historical knowledge and relevance to contemporary issues.










…Inspired by Boal and Brecht, [Ezra] Brain suggests that the nature of political theatre is to disrupt, present a coherent political perspective, and challenge dominant narratives and discourses…From a Marxist perspective, in order for the theatre to be political, it must go beyond entertainment and awareness-building by offering the people a way forward. Performing among community members in Nairobi’s informal settlements, SJCTT introduce[s] unruly protagonists to encourage dialogue amongst the spectators and educate them to consider active participation in politics-which could change their lives for the better.







SJCTT needs to be put in the historical trajectory of links and continuities of revolutionary struggles. Before SJCTT was the University of Nairobi Travelling Theatre (UNTT), and the Kamirithu outdoor theatre that performed Ngugi wa Mirii and Ngugi wa Thiong’o’s play Ngaahika Ndeenda/I Will Marry When I Want. Both performances were projects of the underground movement, the December Twelfth Movement (DTM). Ngugi wa Thiong’o was a member of one of the DTM’s underground cells. The (UNTT) staged various radical plays in high schools all over Kenya. The cast was invariably radical University students from the radical departments in the (UNTT), namely Literature, Law, Political Science, Economics, Sociology, and Religious Studies. We should not forget the Mau Mau’s Kenya Land and Freedom Army’s (KLFA) poems and songs. This Liberation Army still remains the most revolutionary beacon of Kenyan class struggles. These poems and songs were compiled, edited, and translated from the Gikuyu language into English by Maina Wa Kinyatti. As recently as 10-13 September 2026, some of the cast in SJCTT performed at the Kenya National Theatre, Ngugi wa Thiong’o’s   Matigari ma Njiruungi. Ndungi Githuku was the lead actor. He is also the leader of the Field Marshal Band, known for its revolutionary poems and songs.




In Lieu of Conclusion: 

From Mau Mau To Ruto-Must-Go

 

demystified




As I have stated above, the Mau Mau War of Liberation remains the greatest and the main beacon of our revolution. The working peoples of Kenya took up arms to challenge the might of the British Empire. Independence after 78 years of occupation, oppression, and exploitation was a revolution, albeit an ordinary one compared to the great revolutions of the 20th Century. Even those two great revolutions of the 20th Century went through links and continuities of ordinary revolutions.




The attributes of a leader who is a comprador in chief, and the glaring personification of the elite in power is President Museveni. I believe Mahmood Mamdani has interrogated and historicized this issue in the case of Museveni. The outsourcing of the Ugandan Army in Somalia, South Sudan, and the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo are clear examples of a leader of an elite that can second-guess the interests of imperialism and implement its interests. Although Mamdani does not discuss cultural imperialism in Uganda, it is clear Museveni has supported the demands of cultural imperialists in the US and Europe in their quest to get the Parliament of Uganda to enact the draconian Anti-homosexuality Act. The fundamentalist Christian Right in the US and Europe argues that they want to save Africans from the decadence of Western values! Indeed, they say this when they are very ignorant of African values that tolerate and accommodate sexual orientation. These cultural imperialists have always described African values as Satanic. 




President Ruto is the personification of a collective comprador bourgeoisie, a class that has crucial ingredients in the economic, social, cultural, theological, and political spheres. In a country that has deep divisions on ethnicity, individualization of this class could be seen to be against a particular community and thereby enrich the strategies of ethnic divisions by the same comprador class. The entire comprador bourgeoisie has to be historicized and interrogated so that its ingredients are understood. If there is to be personification, it must be to identify the various components of the class and their various respective leaderships. And the link between the comprador bourgeoisie and the imperialist bourgeoisie has to be understood. I believe the Malcolm Xian metaphor of the house niggers is still apt. Indeed, Kenya and the rest of Africa are slave plantations; the ruling elites are a den of house niggers, and the masters of the plantation are the imperialism of the Triad (US, Europe, Japan), including other countries that are in the orbit of imperialism and have interests in Africa, such as China and Russia. President Ruto and the comprador bourgeoisie he leads have supported continuing to allow military bases in Kenya without the participation of Kenyans, that is decreed by the supreme law, the Constitution of Kenya, 2010. He has sent the police to Haiti in defiance of a court order on the issue. The West still pontificates about democracy and the rule of law, but does not comply with our supreme law, finding it abstract and inconvenient, a hallmark of hypocrisy, racism, perfidy, and double standards.




The burning political question in Africa, in my opinion, is the quest for an authentic and patriotic alternative political leaderships. To be such a leadership, it must be at a minimum, anti-imperialist and anti-comprador. It must be a leadership that loves the working people. It must run to the people of Africa for support when it faces the wrath of imperialism. Such leadership has to embrace people-to-people revolutionary Pan-Africanism that includes the African diaspora as the basis of the liberation of Africa. It must be a leadership that understands the status quo of the planet which is unsustainable, unacceptable, and undesirable, and that has to be overthrown. The growing consciousness of global citizens towards identifying the common enemy of the planet we wish to see must be reinforced and supported in this century through a global solidarity against militarism, ecological degradation, sexism, homophobia, domination, exploitation, oppression, and a planet that puts profits before people. Such leadership should participate in the ongoing debates of a socialist planet. These debates seek a consensus on the socialist paradigm that will liberate the planet by interrogating the socialist experiments in the Soviet Union, China, North Korea, Cuba, Vietnam, and other countries where the revolutionary paradigm has been enacted through liberation wars and movements. That project is absolutely critical to identifying what socialist gains have been made, and the exposed weaknesses can be the basis for further discussion that could consolidate a revolutionary theory for implementation.
