title: The End of the Trump Era: The Democratic Sweep of the Midterm Elections
content:
Early this morning, I was woken up by a text from my daughter in Atlanta, nine hours behind Sharjah, UAE, where I’m currently located. Dems are leading, she exclaimed. Can you chat for a quick second? Before I called her, she sent another text, saying, it’s breaking news: Keisha Lance Bottoms is the projected winner as Governor of Georgia. My daughter, who has lived in Atlanta since she went to university there in the early 2000s, was ecstatic beyond measure.




Our celebratory chatter woke up my wife, a political scientist and keen observer of American politics. The ancestors must be smiling, she proclaimed with giddy excitement. We switched on the television and followed the elections on American stations we had access to, including CNN International and Bloomberg, while simultaneously perusing newspapers including The New York Times and The Guardian.




The more we talked and thought about the unfolding election results, I couldn’t help and filtering the elections through Africanist and global lenses, the clearer it became that this stunning blue wave, which polls had been predicting, represented political triumph in five dimensions, what I would the 5Ds: democrats, democracy, diversity, demography, and development.




The Democratic Victory




The Democrats won a resounding victory. Their victories swept the electoral map in Congress and across red states, as they held on to their constituencies. It was a political tsunami that routed President Donald Trump and the Republicans in a stunning rebuke of their failed policies and divisive politics, in which diversionary and inflammatory cultural wars trumped the deteriorating material conditions and interests of the electorate.




Democrats seized both chambers of Congress. Their candidates flipped seven Republican seats in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas, red states some of which had not elected a Democrat in decades. They retained seats in five states, namely, Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, and Virginia.




At the time of writing, the Democrats had flipped 35 seats previously held by Republicans in the House, including multiple seats in states won by Trump by more than 10 points such as Texas, Iowa, Florida, and Pennsylvania, along with key wins in Kentucky, Missouri, Nebraska, Ohio, and Utah. They successfully defended all or nearly all of their incumbent districts , including 22 that were considered vulnerable because Trump carried them by more than 10 points in the 2024 election, and are projected to win 242 to 258 seats when all the votes are counted, 40 more than they need to form a majority.




In a tectonic shift, at the time of writing, with 32 of the 36 seats contested, Democrats had also flipped five state governorships from Republicans in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa, and Nevada, and successfully defended 15 states. They won a total of 29, earning a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010.




So far, with final calls still processing, Democrats have flipped 12 of the 88 state legislative chambers on the ballot from Republican control in Pennsylvania (Senate; they already controlled the House), Wisconsin (both chambers), Arizona (putting Republicans in a legislative minority for the first time in 26 years), North Carolina (House), and drastically broke Republican supermajorities in states like Florida, South Carolina, and Indiana. They successfully defended 25 legislative chambers, including competitive ones in states like Maine, New Mexico, Oregon, and Washington, where they were able to preserve existing Democratic trifectas.




Similarly, Democrats dramatically outperformed Republicans in races for attorney general and secretary of state offices. For the former, the biggest upsets were in Texas and Georgia, while key defensive holds included Nevada and Michigan. Democrats also won the majority of contested secretary of state offices, seizing several from Republicans and holding those they held before.




The Resurgence of Democracy




America’s beleaguered democracy won. Electoral democracy in the United States has always been compromised by gerrymandering, voter suppression, politicization of the judiciary, and the financialization of politics. funding. This is why a conservative outfit like The Economist considers the United States a flawed, rather than a full, democracy compared to its increasingly alienated Western allies such as Canada.




Gerrymandering spectacularly backfired for Republicans. They redrew congressional boundaries across seven states, including Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Alabama, and Louisiana) hoping to flip 15 vulnerable or targeted seats. Democrats succeeded in redrawing maps only in California, seeking 5 pickup opportunities, and Utah an additional seat was created after a court order that struck a Republican map.




Democrats won or held onto at least 10 of the 15 seats targeted by Republican gerrymandering, while successfully defending their own incumbents in heavily redrawn territory. In California and Utah, the Democrats successfully swept all six of their projected pickups, including 3 critical flips in California and won Utah’s court-ordered 1 redistricting seat. This might be one of the most consequential results of the election: the erosion of gerrymandering as a potent political weapon.




Voter suppression involves the imposition of legal, administrative, or logistical measures to discourage or prevent specific segments of the population, mostly racial minorities, from voting. Republicans have become increasingly adept and brazen in trying to use voter purges, strict identification requirements, targeted closure of polling places, restrict mail-in and absentee voting, and raise administrative and psychological barriers through constant and often last-minute changes to voting rules.




Leading to the midterm elections advocacy groups raised the alarm about these tactics, abetted by the erosion of the Voting Rights Act (VRA) by the Supreme Court that in the 2013 Shelby County v. Holder decision gutted pre-clearance provisions of the Act which required states with a demonstrated record of racial discrimination to get federal approval before changing any voting laws or closing polling places, which was reinforced by the 2026 Louisiana v. Callais decision that raised the legal bar for opponents of biased maps to prove intentional malice rather than just discriminatory results.




Cumulatively, these changes to the VRA shifted the burden of fighting voter suppression to more individuals rather than monitoring the state, thereby legalizing voter suppression. However, it backfired as these blatantly anti-democratic measures provoked mass resistance, especially among Black and Latino voters whose early voting turnout surged. The architects of voter suppression were also stalled by defeats in the courts that struck down gerrymandered maps and denied last-minute efforts by the Trump administration to block mail-in ballots and mass purges just before Election Day,




Thus, the highly coordinated voter suppression efforts were neutralized by a combination of historic voter mobilization and decisive judicial interventions, underscoring the fact that popular will and institutional guardrails could withstand the weaponization of voting by anti-democratic forces inspired by the restrictive political covenants of the pre-civil rights era of white supremacy.




Unusual among Western democracies is the scale of the financialization of American politics, which has turned the electoral process into a high-stakes, multi-billion-dollar industry in which megadonors seek to buy political candidates, messaging, and power primarily to serve their interests rather than those of the electorate. They seek to turn elections into empty performative rituals to reproduce state capture and consolidate oligarchic self-enrichment. According to 

OpenSecrets

, the 2026 midterm elections are the most expensive in U.S. history, costing an extraordinary $11.9 billion.




This is the logical consequence of the systematic dismantling of post-Watergate campaign finance laws, in which the Supreme Court ruled that money is a form of constitutionally protected speech. This dates back to the 1976 Buckley v. Valeo decision, which stipulated that while the government could limit direct contributions to candidates to prevent bribery, it could not limit independent spending by individuals or campaigns.




Sanctifying the financialization of elections was the landmark 2010 Citizens United v. FEC decision, which declared that corporations, non-profits, and labor unions have the same First Amendment free speech rights as individual people. Also in the same year, the SpeechNow.org v. FEC and McCutcheon v. FEC decisions facilitated the creation of Super PACs and megadonors as vehicles for massive funding of elections by allowing individuals, corporations, or unions, as long as they didn’t directly coordinate with candidates, to contribute any amount without restriction.




Subsequent Court decisions and election rules legalized pop-up dark money, loosened relations between candidates and Super PACs, and removed restrictions on how much candidates could raise after the elections to pay themselves back for personal loans made to their campaigns. This is the landscape that allowed megadonors such as Elon Musk to donate between $445 and $483 million to Republican candidates and Michael Bloomberg to donate $116 million to Democratic candidates.




Overall, many Republicans relied on large donors while many Democratic candidates boasted about a broader base of small-dollar individual contributions. In the final 10 weeks of the election cycle, Pop-up Super PACs spent a massive $637 million collectively, with Republican-linked late groups outspending Democrats two-to-one while keeping their initial donor identities legally hidden past Election Day.




Financialization undermines American democracy in so far as massive political contributions are increasingly viewed by corporations and billionaires as capital investments that expect a return on investment through targeted tax cuts, regulatory rollbacks, government contracts, or favorable economic policies. This compromises accountability as lawmakers are trapped in a vicious cycle of “permanent fundraising,” shifting their time and accountability away from everyday constituents toward their megadonors.




However, the returns diminish as the media landscape becomes deluged with continuous attack ads, which creates public fatigue, exhaustion, and cynicism about the political process. The results of the election would seem to suggest limits to the financial capture of elections by megadonors. In many cases, their candidates in the primaries of both parties lost, and in the elections the billions spent by the titans of the tech industry and the American Israel Political Action Committee (AIPAC) to support Republicans amounted to a spectacular waste of money, showing the limits of buying democracy for a population fired up by their own economic and existential interests.




The Triumph of Diversity




Disparaged diversity won. There will be more minority governors, senators and representatives in Congress than ever before in American history. Altogether, the lone Black governor, Wes Moore of Maryland who won his re-election, will be joined by four new Black governors: three of them Democrats, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black female governor in U.S. history, David Crowley, who made history as Wisconsin’s first Black governor, Aaron Ford, who flipped the Nevada governorship out of Republican hands, and one Republican, Byron Donalds, who became Florida’s first Black governor.




In addition, two Latinos were elected Democratic governors: Gina Hinojosa, who pulled off a historic upset by defeating three-term incumbent Republican Greg Abbott, becoming the first Latina governor in Texas history, and Xavier Becerra, who became California’s first Latino governor since 1875. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland, a Democrat, made history as the first Native American female governor of a U.S. state.




In the meantime, 12 white women were elected as governors, four for the first time: Amy Acton (D-OH), who defeated the insufferable Vivek Ramaswamy to become the first woman governor in Ohio’s history, Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), who became the first female governor in Minnesota’s history, Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), who also made history as the first female governor of Tennessee, and Kelly Ayotte (R-NH), who retained Republican control in a highly competitive race. Eight other incumbent white women governors retained their seats, six of whom are Democrats and two Republicans.




As for senators, two newly elected African American and African-descended senators, Juliana Stratton (D-IL) and Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) will join five sitting African American senators who were not up for election this cycle: Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD) and Tim Scott (R-SC). As for Latinos, the newly elected Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) and re-elected incumbent Alex Padilla (D-CA) will serve alongside four sitting senators Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Ben Ray Luján (D-NM), Ted Cruz (R-TX), and Bernie Moreno (R-OH). The Senate will also have one new Native American senator, Peggy Flanagan (D-MN), as well as three sitting Asian American Democratic senators, Andy Kim (NJ), Tammy Duckworth (IL), and Mazie Hirono (HI). At the time of writing the election in Alaska has not been declared, and the democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, is Native American.




While we await the release of all House seats, it is more than likely that the number of minority representatives will be historically unprecedented. Among the highlights is the fact that Hakeem Jeffries is slated to become the first Black Speaker of the House. Another Black interesting development is that the number of House members who are African-born immigrants or first-generation children of African immigrants will grow.




Twenty-nine-year-old Melat Kiros, born in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, a Democratic Socialist, will join Ilhan Omar, born in Somalia, as the second African-born woman in the House, and the first Black woman from Colorado and Gen Z. In Maryland, 32-year-old Adrian Boafo, a son of Ghanaian immigrants, won his House seat, where he will join Joe Neguse, a son of Eritrean immigrants who won his reelection in Colorado, and Gabe Amo, a son of Ghanaian and Liberian parents, won his reelection in Rhode Island.




Other remarkable electoral victories include from the Asian American community Pia Dandiya (D-FL), a first-generation Indian-American, who enjoyed one of the most high-profile flips of this election cycle in a gerrymandered Republican district. From the Native American community, there is Claire Valdez (D-NY), who ran on a progressive platform and became the first Native American woman representative from the state of New York. Among the Latino community, Denise Powell (D-NE) flipped a Republican seat to become the first Hispanic representative ever elected to Congress from Nebraska, while Emily Randall (D-WA) made history as the first openly LGBTQ+ Latina ever elected to the United States Congress.




The diversity of the newly elected state governors and members of Congress constitutes a blistering rebuke of Trump’s chaotic, crass, corrupt, and cruel presidency, of resurgent white supremacy, of MAGA’s racist, reactionary and retrograde efforts to turn back to Reconstruction-era America. It also throws a harsh light on companies, institutions, and organizations, including businesses, media houses, universities, and law firms that unashamedly and hurriedly abandon diversity, equity and inclusion, often preemptively obeying executive orders or political pronouncements by Trump and his minions that went beyond the law.




The Power of Demography




Shifting demography won. It is often not well understood or fully appreciated that massive transformation of the American population is a product of the Civil Rights Movement. Three landmark laws were passed in response to civil rights struggles led by African Americans against centuries-long oppression, persecution, and marginalization.




The first was the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, and officially ended legal segregation in public places and schools. Second, the Voting Rights Act was passed in 1965, which banned discriminatory voting practices that had been systematically used in southern states to disenfranchise Black voters. Third, the Immigration and Nationality Act in 1965, which abolished the “national origins” quota system that had severely restricted immigration from non-European countries since the 1920s, opening immigration to people from Africa, Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean.




The backlash against the changes wrought by these laws provoked racist revanchism among some whites unable to compete without the privileges of whiteness. They were cynically mobilized by radical conservatives increasingly coalesced in the Republican Party, whose conservative ideologues were burnished by a network of well-funded right-wing and populist institutions including think tanks, the media, professional associations, and even universities where affirmative action combined with neoliberalism created intense, racialized competition for the symbolic capital of access, certification, and professional status.




This explains why elite universities quickly embraced judicial assaults against affirmative action because they never believed in it; it only served a performative role, which lost its currency with the resurgence of a populist backlash against the Great Recession and the Obama Presidency, which turbocharged fears of white replacement. These fears fueled anti-immigration sentiments, culminating in the militarized brutalities of ICE raids in Democratic-led American cities.




The results of the midterm elections represent a repudiation of the cultural and civic wars of the American right, a powerful indictment of the governance failures of contemporary American right-wing populism, which has failed to address the pressing economic, social, technological, political, and geopolitical challenges facing the nation in a rapidly changing and highly competitive world marked by multilateralism and the relative decline of Euro-America.




America’s populism combines three strands: the age-old reflexes of white supremacy, the anti-immigration crusade of European right-wing movements, and the historic lessons of white minority rule from apartheid South Africa, eagerly financed and popularized by the South African mafia led by Elon Musk that has constructed the perverse myth of white genocide in post-apartheid South Africa that Trump and his MAGA base have fervently embraced.




When comprehensive election data is available, I expect that it will show racial minorities, women and young people, including those who gravitated to Trump in 2024, believing his grandiose lies and false promises, were in the forefront of the political tsunami that has swept the Republican Party from congressional power. Those who voted for Trump in 2024, either out of ideological conviction or in the vain hope that his retrofitted administration would improve their lives and livelihoods, have been rudely disappointed over the past two years.




Among Trump’s supporters in 2024, there were 69 percent of white men without a college degree, 53 percent of white women, 46 to 48 percent of Latinos, 37 to 40 percent of Asian Americans, 20 to 21 percent of Black men. Sequels are rarely better than the original show, so it is with Trump. He returned to power freed from institutional guardrails, eager to exact retribution on his enemies, real and imagined, surrounded by spineless and enabling sycophants, and more erratic and opinionated than ever, basking in his omniscience and omnipresence.




His administration took away reproductive rights from women, emasculated his white male supporters, including young men with diminishing wages and prospects for enjoying the American dream. It also ensnared Latinos with the otherization of draconian immigration crackdowns, and dismantled the promises of the model minority myth for Asian Americans as they faced rising racism. Further, it decimated opportunities for Black men in an economy waging war on Black employment and businesses in the crusade against DEI.




Above all, it raised the cost of living for everyone through his inane tariff policies and unprovoked war with Iran, as he simultaneously enriched his wealthy, feckless cronies and cheerleaders with unconscionable tax cuts and indulged in unprecedented corruption of any president in American history.




The Seductions of Decency




The desire for decency won. As they say, reeled from the shenanigans under the unbelievably inept and self-destructive second Trump administration, more and more Americans yearned for something better. They became exhausted by its relentless assaults to their sense of decency, by the mindlessness of its gratuitous meanness, and the endless embarrassment from the cringeworthy idiocy of their globally despised president. Americans, like other people, derive part of their national pride from the international reputation of their leaders. Trump has brought Americans widespread shame.




The midterm elections gave them an opportunity to exact their revenge, against the despicable misogyny, the wanton racism, the economic incompetence, the daily spectacles of vengefulness, the deepening partisanship and polarization, the public incivility and the sickening abandonment of moral values, the incessant pathological lying. They sought the ennobling possibilities of community, dialogue, and dignity.




The electorate also responded to the quality and conduct of the candidates. Many of the Republican candidates, some of whom were strongly supported by Trump, were not only patently unqualified but also known to be corrupt and engaged in vicious personal attacks mimicking their godfather, Trump, whereas the Democrats were focused on issues.




The Imperatives of Development




The search for development won. As in other parts of the world in both the developed and developing countries, the working and middle classes strive for the well-being and social stability that comes from living wages, access to good education, healthcare, social services and public infrastructure. They resent deepening inequalities, the unelected and unaccountable power of oligopolies and obscenely rich oligarchs, who see themselves as masters of the universe.




Especially unpopular are the tech bros, whose data centers are gobbling up massive water and energy resources, raising the utility bills of local communities, threatening jobs and the future of humanity in a mindless and unregulated chase for super-intelligence whose dangers are poorly understood or appreciated.




In this election, the legacies of more than forty years of neoliberalism, reframed by the Great Recession and Covid-19 pandemic, were on trial, so were cuts to healthcare and other welfare programs. In the meantime, people saw levels of national indebtedness rise, surpassing $40 trillion, and military expenditures on a new forever war in Iran exploded. At the same time, the war brought higher oil and gas prices and for other commodities whose production and flows have been severely disrupted by the war in West Asia. According to The New York Times, every demographic group, including White voters, Hispanic voters, Black voters, and young voters, moved left.




The affordability crisis, emblematic of the broken promises of the neoliberal development model, is evident in many parts of the world. Europe has been engulfed by escalating protests led by Gen Z and working people. This is true in many parts of the Global South as well. The political ramifications vary as some incumbent populist governments fall, for example in Hungary and Serbia, while elsewhere liberal regimes are threatened by rising disaffection and disorder that empowers populist forces as evident in Germany and France. In Brazil, the incumbent left-wing government of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva survived the insurgent crusade of the populist right wing of the Bolsonaros, who fancied themselves as replicas of Trump in Latin America.




With this election, Trump has become the Bolsonaro of North America, his party decisively rejected by the electorate. Trump is now officially a lame duck president, a fate that befalls most presidents after they lose the midterm elections, which is often the case, especially during their second term. But Trump is different from his predecessors in that he is the first president in a century to serve two nonconsecutive terms.




Perhaps even more crucial is that this might portend something much larger: the collapse of the MAGA, the end of the Trump era that has dominated American politics during the past decade ever since he entered the race for the presidency in 2016. Trump has been a consequential president, not because his policies were good for America, let alone the world, but because he fundamentally transformed American politics and institutions, articulating and accelerating trends that long antedated him.




The Challenges and Possibilities of Change




Many analysts are concerned about what a lame duck Trump might mean for the world, in so far as many of his predecessors turned to foreign policy to burnish their legacy. Trump has no international legacy to build on. But he can cause a lot of damage as he lashes out against his political diminution and inquisition of his policies by a Democratic Congress in reckless foreign adventures including restarting the Iran war and embark on regime change in Cuba and elsewhere, or reignite his disputes with Canada and America’s NATO allies, collude with Russia and China to divide the world into three great power spheres.




As to be expected, the Democratic sweep has triggered a blame game among Republicans. For example, Vice President J.D. Vance blames the loss on the Iran war, in a veiled criticism of his boss. This presages the possibility that defiance, or at least disaffection and distancing from Trump’s policies, might grow.




But the victorious Democrats will also be under enormous pressure to check Trump and meet the demands and expectations of impatient voters. The president will wield veto power over their legislative initiatives, which would require them to work with chastened Republicans to override. They need to work on the cost of living crisis by rolling back tariffs, dealing seriously with government debt, which would require both raising taxes and entitlement reform, ending the war in Iran, regulating the AI industry, strengthening job training and improving education, robustly dealing with the climate crisis, and helping provide health care beyond the limited measures of the Affordable Care Act or Obamacare.




I’m not sure if Democrats are up to the task. Not only is their tent in the new Congress more ideologically diverse than ever, but the party establishment is also timid, beholden to large donors and lobbyists, and they seem invested in the myth of the political center as the best political space to occupy. They need to abandon meaningless centrism and embark on bold, popular programs to improve the well-being of ordinary people, and worry less about the rich and their ideologues in the media and academy.




They also need to manage America’s adjustment to one major power among others in a multilateral world. American supremacy, indeed, imperialism, after World War II brought the country great benefits to its economy and standard of living. But it has now become an unsustainable drag on its economy. The party that manages America’s transition and its transformation into a nation that is not permanently embroiled in foreign wars will be good for itself and the world. Imperialism at home and racism at home reinforce each other.




One critical international relationship that is likely to become central in the United States is the relationship with Israel, a country that has an oversized impact on American foreign policy because of the role of the Israeli lobby. The fierce criticisms of America’s subservience to Israeli interests, what some regard as the tail-wagging-the-dog syndrome, by many Democrats, especially the Democratic Socialists, and among younger Americans, will force changes. Preemptively, on the morning of the election, Trump announced that the United States will cease providing its newest $4 billion annual aid to Israel.




It is unlikely that U.S. – Africa relations will change much given that the executive branch controls foreign affairs. However, with long-time Africa policy advocate Senator Chris Coons (D-DE) poised to take over as Chairman of the powerful Senate Foreign Relations Committee, there may be renewed scrutiny on foreign aid and agency cuts, efforts to reset relations with African nations, including South Africa, that have been battered by indifference, transactional diplomacy, and a focus on the extraction of critical minerals, data, and other resources, and a reevaluation of visa restrictions and travel bans.




America must strive to become an inclusive non-racial democracy. All this is a tall order. But Democrats must use their new power strategically and act decisively. If they fail to do so, the voters will punish them in two years, and the musical chairs of political switcharoo will come back to haunt them to the detriment of the American people.

The End of the Trump Era: The Democratic Sweep of the Midterm Elections

author: Scott Timcke
title: The Stories Shaping Africa’s AI Future
content:
In the boardrooms of Addis Ababa and the tech hubs of Nairobi, a new worldmaking project is underway. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the central arenas where African states negotiate their position in an unequal global order. To speak of “AI in Africa” is not simply to describe the arrival of a technology, but to encounter a set of competing discursive frames through which political desires, developmental ambitions, ethical claims, and governance priorities are translated into technical agendas. As national strategies and regional protocols are rolled out, what comes into view is a struggle over how Africa is imagined within this machine age, and what kinds of futures that imagination makes thinkable.




These frames are not simply different ways of describing a new technology. They are competing scripts for what Africa is, what AI is for, and who ought to shape its future. Some cast the continent as a site of leapfrogging and renewal; others as a zone of exposure, extraction, sovereignty, moral repair, or improvised adaptation. Each brings some actors and possibilities into focus while pushing others to the margins. That is why the issue is not only what AI means for Africa, but what pictures of Africa are being called into view through AI discourse.




The first terrain is shaped by promise and protection. One of the most pervasive registers is promissory. In the African renaissance 2.0 frame, visible in the 

AU Continental AI Strategy

, AI appears as a 

leapfrogging

 device through which Africa can bypass the chokepoint of traditional industrialization and enter prosperity through technical modernization. Here, the ethical subject is the developmental state or planner charged with delivering growth, inclusion, and renewal. What comes into view is capacity, competitiveness, and beneficial transformation. What recedes from view are the historical and political-economic conditions that make acceleration so attractive in the first place: debt, infrastructural dependence, uneven ownership, and the possibility that AI may deepen rather than overcome inherited asymmetries.




Running alongside this is a protective register. In this vulnerability frame, Africa is not late but exposed to surveillance, bias, exclusion, and systems introduced into settings where safeguards are weak and redress is limited. As the 

CIVICUS report on AI surveillance in Africa

 suggests, the issue is not only future risk but already existing forms of technologically mediated harm. The ethical subject here is the harm-bearing population—the data subject, precarious worker, surveilled citizen, and linguistically marginal user most likely to absorb the costs of badly governed AI. This frame is ethically indispensable because it foregrounds rights, harm, and institutional fragility, including the uneven but growing architecture of data protection on the continent. Its limit, however, is that it can cast Africa chiefly as a site to be protected rather than one from which technological futures are actively contested and shaped.




A second terrain is shaped by structure and sovereignty. Alongside these promissory and protective registers sits a more structural critique. In the 

anti-colonial frame

, AI appears as a socio-technical order built through unequal material relations: not only data extraction, but also mineral supply chains, outsourced labor, environmental degradation, foreign-owned infrastructures, and asymmetrical control over the institutions that govern digital life. From this perspective, Africa is not outside the AI order looking in; it is already deeply inserted into it, though often on subordinated terms. The ethical subject is the dispossessed worker, community, or polity whose labor, resources, and data are drawn into AI systems while ownership and value are captured elsewhere. What becomes visible is the political economy of AI—an approach that makes it harder to sustain the comforting idea that Africa’s main problem is simply one of readiness or delayed entry. But the frame has limits. In foregrounding dispossession, it can flatten internal differentiation, externalize agency too completely, and become so totalizing that the uneven realities of negotiation and strategic inhabitation recede from view.




The sovereignty frame shifts the question from extraction to control: AI is cast as a problem of authority over infrastructure, procurement, standards, and rulemaking, a concern visible in South Africa’s 

National Data and Cloud Computing Policy

. Its appeal lies in insisting that African states must govern technological systems in the public interest rather than merely consume them on external terms; the ethical subject is the sovereign polity, imagined above all as the state charged with authoring technological futures on its own terms. But sovereignty should not be romanticized. Declaring authority is not the same as possessing material control, especially where states remain dependent on foreign cloud infrastructures, imported models, consultants, and opaque procurement chains. Equally, this frame can too quickly presume the state to be the vehicle of emancipation.




A third terrain is shaped by ethics and language. Beneath these macro-struggles lie cultural and ethical frames. In the 

Ubuntu

 frame, Africa appears as a moral resource: a source of relational vocabularies of dignity, community, interdependence, and solidarity that unsettle liberal individualism in mainstream AI ethics. At its strongest, this frame asks what kind of human subject AI presupposes and produces. Its ethical subject is the person-in-community, understood less as an isolated rights-bearer than as a being constituted through relations of community, solidarity, and mutual recognition. At its weakest, it risks remaining 

symbolically reparative and romantic

 rather than politically disruptive: 

a moral vocabulary that pluralizes AI ethics without redistributing authority

 over infrastructure, capital, or standards.




The linguistic justice frame relocates the issue to language, depicting Africa as linguistically marginalized. Initiatives such as 

Lelapa

 and 

Masakhane

 insist that language is not a neutral interface but a site through which recognition and opportunity are distributed in digital life. An AI system that cannot adequately process Yoruba, Wolof, or Zulu does more than inconvenience its speakers; it helps reproduce a hierarchy in which some languages, and the worlds they carry, are made 

computationally peripheral

. The ethical subject here is the speaker, the language community, and the knower whose access to digital life is mediated through systems not built with them in mind. Yet linguistic inclusion alone does not resolve ownership, infrastructure, or power. An AI that speaks African languages can still be embedded in extractive or externally governed systems.




A final terrain is shaped by markets and adaptation. The market pragmatist frame, visible in the 

African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Protocol on Digital Trade

, casts Africa as a jurisdictional space to be made legible to capital—a continent whose frictions must be reduced so that innovation, trade, and platform expansion can move more easily across borders through harmonization, regulatory alignment, and investment readiness. Here, the ethical subject is the investor, firm, regulator, and entrepreneurial ecosystem said to require clear rules and scalable markets. What becomes visible is efficiency, interoperability, and growth. What recedes from view is the fact that harmonization is never merely technical. It can distribute advantage, privileging certain actors over others, and can also displace questions of labor and ownership while eclipsing democratic accountability behind the smoother language of market access.




The frugal innovator frame—the 

jua kali

 of tech—foregrounds small-scale, improvised solutions that work offline, on cheap devices, and in low-resource settings. 

Lelapa AI’s InkubaLM

 is the sharpest contemporary example. This frame’s appeal lies in refusing the assumption that meaningful technical work must begin from abundance. Africa appears as inventive under pressure, capable of repurposing constraints into forms of practical intelligence. The ethical subject is the builder, bricoleur, local entrepreneur, and community improviser who makes systems work where industrial-scale infrastructures are absent. What becomes apparent is creativity, resilience, and situated responsiveness. But it can also romanticize necessity, making scarcity look like authenticity rather than a political condition to be transformed. It can overstate what ingenuity can compensate for and understate the need for public investment, industrial policy, and durable institutional support.




In the end, what matters about these eight frames is not whether any one of them finally tells the truth about Africa and AI. It is that each organizes moral and political attention differently—foregrounding development while muting dependency, naming extraction and harm while narrowing agency, valorizing language and ethics without redistributing material authority. As a constellation of concerns, they reveal less a single African AI trajectory than a struggle over what Africa is imagined and allowed to be in technological modernity.




That is why AI in Africa is not just about chips, code, or competitiveness. It is about who gets to architect the future, under what terms, and in whose interests. The stakes are not simply adoption or regulation, but the representational politics through which certain subjects, institutions, and futures become thinkable while others fall from view.




Yet these frames do not only describe Africa; they help make it where they are taken up. This is the worldmaking with which we began. What a frame brings into view becomes what institutions are built to serve, and what it lets recede goes ignored. Nor do the frames work alone. They overlap and prop one another up: sovereignty talk can leverage the anti-colonial critique, market pragmatism needs the renaissance’s promissory optimism, and the frugal innovator’s ingenuity is enlisted to soften the very scarcity it works within. The future, then, will not be settled by one script defeating the others, but by which come to dominate the mixture—and whose interests that mixture ends up serving—as it hardens into the continent’s legal, institutional, and material infrastructure. Whether this moment marks a structural shift or the repetition of old patterns turns on that.

author: Alf Gunvald Nilsen
title: Southern Authoritarian Populism
content:
The early twenty-first century is a time of monsters in the Global South. 




What do these monsters look like? 




Let me begin with those at work closest to home, namely in post-apartheid South Africa, where I live and work. 




On 30 June 2026, the country’s streets were awash with hate. In cities like Johannesburg, Durban, and Pretoria, as well as in smaller towns, tens of thousands of people – mostly poor and working-class Black South Africans – marched behind slogans blaming undocumented migrants from other African countries for unemployment, crime, failing public services, and drug addiction. Their rallying cry was simple: 

Abahambe!

 – They Must Go! The day itself – 30 June – was the “deadline” that xenophobic organizations had set for undocumented migrants to leave the country. In the months leading up to this date, these organizations mobilized popular support for the idea of expulsion across the country. As the deadline approached, thousands of African foreigners flocked to their diplomatic missions to seek emergency repatriation. At least four people were killed before the marches took place, and countless others lost their livelihoods or fled their communities in fear.




Much about this moment was uniquely South African. Above all, the fact that the targets of hate, violence, and murder are Black African migrants, not White migrants from the Global North like me, has been a constant across similar upsurges in 2008, 2015, and 2019. This has led the Cameroonian scholar Achille Mbembe to speak of Afrophobia – a fear and hatred specifically of the Black African Other – as a distinctive predicament of South Africa’s post-apartheid order.  




Yet it was also something more. Across the Global South, we have witnessed the rise of a monstrous far-right politics that rallies majoritarian people-nations against ominous Others while normalizing increasingly authoritarian political orders. This far right takes multiple forms: in some cases, such as Erdogan’s Turkey or Narendra Modi’s India, it manifests as 

entrenched

 far-right regimes with a firm grip on political power; in other cases, such as Brazil and the Philippines, it has found expression in 

emergent

 formations that have won power electorally without succeeding in consolidating durable regimes but still maintain a strong presence in politics and society. In yet other cases, such as South Africa, the far right is present in more embryonic forms, as reactionary social movements and parties that have begun to make their sway felt in the political domain and throughout the social fabric.




I refer to these political monstrosities as Southern authoritarian populism, and the purpose of this essay is to provide a politically enabling diagnosis of it. My argument is not simply that authoritarian populism has appeared in different countries across the Global South. It is that these diverse trajectories are part of an interconnected turn toward the far right across the Global South. Rather than looking at these regimes, parties, and movements in ways that make despair convincing, I want to present a reading that makes hope possible.




This begs an obvious question: where do we find the critical intellectual resources that enable us to untangle the politics of the new far right in the Global South? My search for an answer to this question has led me to two major conclusions. The first of these is that standard academic perspectives on autocratization and far-right populism have little to offer us. Studies of autocratization show us how strongman leaders eviscerate democratic institutions, procedures, and norms. Populism studies have painted vivid portraits of how these leaders perform far-right politics as a distinctive political style. However, neither of these perspectives can tell us much about the real questions we should be asking if we want to understand Southern authoritarian populism from a progressive and radical perspective and in a way that allows us to counteract it. 




So what are the questions that we have to ask? They are questions about the political economy that has generated the precarious working classes that align with the far right; about the structures of feeling, simultaneously aspirational and anxious, that the far right has been capable of harnessing within this political economy; and they are questions about the ideological work that articulates diverse social forces into revanchist people-nations and produces consent from below to projects that ultimately serve the interests of economic and political elites.




This brings me to the second conclusion I have reached in thinking about these questions, which is that the work of the Jamaican-born cultural theorist, public intellectual, and activist Stuart Hall stands us in good stead as we search for the kind of insurgent epistemic gain that allows us a glimpse of possible points of entry into a counterhegemonic response to these far-right formations. 




What I draw from Stuart Hall is, above all, his commitment to what he called conjunctural analysis. Conjunctural analysis is a way of making sense of moments of deep organic crisis, when accumulation strategies stagnate, existing forms of governance and political representation begin to break down, and dominant ideologies no longer secure popular consent. These are not separate developments. Rather, they are contradictions that are knotted together in conjunctures where a given form of hegemony unravels. This throws up a political terrain on which social movements from below contend with movements from above as powerful and wealthy groups act to remake their hegemony. 




Hall called these movements from above hegemonic projects. Their aim is not simply to win elections but to remake society. They dismantle old hegemonic formations, forge new historic blocs that unite elite and popular forces, cultivate new political identities and new forms of common sense, and ultimately find pathways from civil society to the state where they implement programmes that reshape society. Practising his work at a safe distance from the high-level abstractions of Marxist theory, Hall focused on understanding how exactly these hegemonic projects do their work, precisely so that it might be possible to counteract them. 




Hall never defined conjunctural analysis in the abstract. Instead, he practised it. Above all, he practised it through a sustained critical engagement with how the New Right in Britain, helmed by Margaret Thatcher, articulated what he called authoritarian populism as a hegemonic project. This project transformed British economic life, politics, and society in crucial ways during the 1970s and 1980s. 




I don’t intend to map the arc of this body of work in this essay, but I’ll outline its main insights as these are eminently useful for thinking about the new far right in the Global South. Authoritarian populism, Hall argued, emerged in response to the crisis of post-war capitalism and the hegemonic order that had governed it. Breaking with the post-war settlement built around Keynesianism and the welfare state, the New Right fused advocacy for a turn to free markets with a reactionary ideology centred on a conservative imaginary of the nation, the family, order, and authority. Within this hegemonic project, the British people were imagined as a hardworking, law-abiding, and quintessentially White majority, against its Other – an enemy within composed of countercultural outsiders, welfare scroungers, left-wing radicals, and a criminal underclass of Black urban youth. This enemy would be brought to heel by the long arm of the law, so that the deserving people-nation could live safely and securely and benefit from the magic of the marketplace. 




As a hegemonic project, Thatcher’s authoritarian populism was incredibly successful. From 1979 onwards, Thatcher and the Conservative Party won three consecutive general elections and implemented a profound neoliberalization of Britain’s political economy. That restructuring is why Britain today is one of the most unequal societies in the Global North, where the richest 10 per cent of the population hold some 45 per cent of the country’s total wealth, while the poorest 50 per cent are left with as little as 10 per cent. Deep inequality is precisely what neoliberal success looks like.




The key to this success was the ability of authoritarian populism to construct a historic bloc that crossed class lines. Thatcher’s project was not just supported by the country’s economic elites; it also won substantial support among working-class voters, at the same time as it defeated organized labour, above all in the miners’ strike in the mid-1980s. Hall was very clear in his analysis that this achievement was not the result of some kind of false consciousness laying siege to the British working class. On the contrary, authoritarian populism won active consent far beyond the country’s elite classes because it spoke to 

real

 problems, 

real

 lived experiences, and 

real

 contradictions that working-class communities struggled with. It did so not only at the level of material interests, but also at the level of identity, subjectivity, and feeling. In this way, and through sustained ideological work, it articulated a new popular common sense that aligned ordinary people’s aspirations and anxieties with the policies and class strategies of the right.




Hall’s methodological ethos provides a point of departure for understanding the time of monsters in the Global South. 




My argument begins with a simple claim: far-right regimes, parties, and movements are advancing across the Global South because we are passing through an interregnum in which, as Antonio Gramsci put it, the old is dying and the new cannot be born. What do I mean by this? I mean the following: the present is not a moment in which the Global South is rising. On the contrary, it is a moment of deep transregional crisis. 




But isn’t this claim counter-intuitive? Over the past three decades, countries across the Global South have become increasingly important in the world economy, and they have become more assertive at the level of geopolitics as the old Western-dominated order has given way to a multipolar world. Indeed, many have celebrated these developments as marking a new phase of anti-imperial advance in the early twenty-first century. So why do I insist that we are living through a Southern interregnum instead?




Let’s start with the fact that middle-income countries in the Global South are home to more than 70 per cent of all poor people in the world today. This poverty is not the result of an absolute lack of resources. On the contrary, it is the product of how the gains from economic growth have been distributed – in short, poverty in Southern middle-income countries is the result of inequality. Since the 1990s, the richest 10 per cent in these countries have captured an ever-larger share of national income while accumulating a vastly disproportionate share of private wealth. At the same time, the share of national income going to workers in the form of wages has steadily declined. That is hardly accidental. It is the predictable outcome of neoliberal growth strategies that have depended on the super-exploitation of labour.




The result is that working-class life across much of the Global South has become increasingly precarious. Wages are low. Stable employment is scarce. Social mobility has stalled. For millions of people, dignity and security remain elusive despite decades of economic growth. At the same time, many middle-income countries remain trapped in the lower reaches of global value chains, competing through cheap labour rather than technological upgrading. In short, neoliberalism has entered a zombie phase. Its developmental promise has been exhausted, but it continues to stagger on.




Across the Global South, disillusionment with zombie neoliberalism has erupted in successive waves of popular protest, from the Arab uprisings of the early 2010s to today’s Gen Z revolts across Asia and Africa. Here we arrive at the heart of the Southern interregnum: a profound disconnection between the two imperatives that every capitalist state must somehow reconcile – accumulation and legitimation. This crisis of legitimation demands a response from above. Southern authoritarian populism is precisely that. It is a hegemonic project that seeks to rebuild consent for a neoliberal order whose developmental promise has long since died, but which stubbornly refuses to lie down. 




How does Southern authoritarian populism do this? The answer to this question will emerge from a comparative conjunctural analysis of the 

entrenched

 form of these hegemonic projects (Turkey and India, where Erdogan and Modi have established durable regimes that have transformed both state and economy) with their 

emergent

 form (the Philippines and Brazil, where authoritarian populism has held power more tenuously, but remains a potent political force) and their more embryonic form in South Africa. 




Southern authoritarian populism operates with ideologies that pivot on constructions of the people-nation as an authentic, virtuous collective defined through markers such as religion, race, ethnicity, moral character, or sexuality. For example, in Erdogan’s Turkey, the people-nation – the 

millet

 – is portrayed as consisting of pious and hardworking Sunni Muslims with deep roots in the country’s Anatolian heartland and Ottoman past. In Modi’s India, the people-nation is the country’s Hindu majority, which the ruling party and the wider Hindu nationalist movement want to restore to its ancient civilizational glory. For both Duterte in the Philippines and Bolsonaro in Brazil, the people-nation was imagined as consisting of decent, diligent, and, above all, law-abiding citizens.




These people-nations are portrayed as being under threat from a range of internal enemies that are braided together into a single antagonistic Other that may encompass religious minorities, subordinated racial and ethnic groups, queer communities, criminals, political dissenters, and old corrupt elites. In Erdogan’s authoritarian populism, the main antagonists of the people-nation are westernized metropolitan elites and a democratic opposition that is stigmatized as terrorists. Modi’s Hindu nationalism posits India’s Muslim minority as the principal enemy within, while Duterte and Bolsonaro trained their sights on criminalized underclasses – alleged drug users and dealers in the case of the former, and the racialized urban poor in the case of the latter.




Within these ideological frames, the coercive capacities of the state are represented as necessary instruments for protecting the people-nation from these perceived threats. This has very real repressive and violent consequences, whether in the form of judicial persecution of political opponents, legislation that violates minority rights, vigilante attacks on minority groups, or, in the case of Duterte’s Philippines, an extrajudicial war on drugs that resulted in as many as 30,000 killings. More fundamentally, this ideological representation of coercion becomes a vehicle of legitimation. It produces a popular authoritarian consensus in which strongman leaders appear as the only figures capable of restoring order, defending the people-nation, and delivering renewed prosperity.




To serve its hegemonic ends, Southern authoritarian populism puts these ideologies to work by articulating diverse social forces into historic blocs capable of underpinning bids for political power. This work is carried out through organizational infrastructures that exist both in the form of real-world networks – such as the century-old Hindu nationalist movement in India and the more recent but similarly extensive Islamist movement in Turkey – and in digital spaces, where social media platforms enable these projects to reach and mobilize the people-nation. 




The defining feature of these historic blocs is that they cut across class lines. In varying degrees, Southern authoritarian populism has consistently won the consent of poor and working-class groups. In Turkey, voter support for Erdogan’s AKP has never fallen below 46 per cent among the poorest quintile and 39 per cent among the second poorest quintile of the electorate. In India, the BJP has increased electoral support from the working poor, Dalits, and lower-caste groups to such an extent that the party commands more than 40 per cent of the Hindu vote. Although Duterte’s campaign initially resonated most strongly with Filipino elites and the middle classes, his victory ultimately depended on support from the urban poor. Bolsonaro, meanwhile, won Brazil’s 2018 election by making major inroads among working-class voters who had experienced modest upward mobility during the years of Workers’ Party rule. 




This has happened despite the fact that these hegemonic projects have remained firmly committed to neoliberal economic policies that have deepened inequality and precarity. How do we explain this paradox? To answer that question, we have to consider something that Stuart Hall took very seriously, namely structures of feeling. More specifically, we have to understand the structures of feeling that saturate the lifeworlds of precarious working classes in an age of zombie neoliberalism. 




Ethnographic studies of working-class communities across Turkey, India, the Philippines, Brazil, and the Global South more broadly reveal a remarkably consistent pattern. Life under zombie neoliberalism is animated by an entanglement of anxiety and aspiration. People aspire to upward mobility and material affluence, believing they can attain it by acting as entrepreneurs in the marketplace. At the same time, they live with the constant fear of sliding into absolute poverty – of losing what little they have and the status that comes with it.




Across the Global South, popular entrepreneurial aspirations are unlikely to be realized precisely because of how neoliberal markets work. Conversely, anxieties about social decline are a clear and present danger. All it takes is a global market downturn that wipes out a fragile micro-enterprise, or a corporate decision to relocate production in pursuit of higher profits that costs someone their job. 




It is on this terrain that Southern authoritarian populism does its most important ideological work. It shapes aspirational affects into commitment to the strongman leaders who promise to guide the people-nation on its path to greater prosperity. The dreams deferred will come true, if only the people remain loyal to the leader, the state and the government, the party, the movement. It channels anxious sentiments into resentment against the Others of the people-nation, who are cast as the folk devils responsible for holding ordinary people back and taking from them what is rightfully theirs. If only the folk-devil is defeated, expelled, or erased, the people-nation will rise to greatness. In this way, structures of feeling are translated into a reactionary and revanchist common sense.




This is precisely what happened in Brazil. In the urban peripheries of São Paulo and other major cities, many working-class families had experienced modest improvements in their lives during the years of Workers’ Party government. They bought household appliances, sent their children to university, and began to imagine a more secure future. But when economic crisis struck in the mid-2010s, many of those gains unravelled. Jobs disappeared, debt mounted, violent crime remained pervasive, and optimism gave way to anxiety. That anxiety soon found political expression on the country’s streets, where mass demonstrations gathered momentum around demands for the ouster of President Dilma Rousseff of the Workers’ Party. 




As these protests crystallized into a broader wave of anti-

petismo

 – hostility towards the Workers’ Party and everything it had come to represent – Jair Bolsonaro emerged as the figurehead of Brazil’s new far right. His appeal extended beyond denunciations of the Workers’ Party. He redirected frustration towards the figure of the criminal. Bolsonaro promised that decent, law-abiding Brazilians could once again prosper if only the state unleashed its coercive power against those cast as dangerous vagabonds. This vengeful promise resonated with millions of Brazilians and Bolsonaro went on to win 55 per cent of the vote in the 2018 presidential election. This is how Southern authoritarian populism articulates structures of feeling into reactionary common sense and how reactionary common sense becomes electoral power.




Bolsonaro’s grip on power did not last. After losing the 2022 presidential election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the Workers’ Party, he refused to accept defeat. He is now serving a 27-year prison sentence for his role in orchestrating the failed coup attempt that followed. Duterte, too, is now out of office, although under very different circumstances. Following the end of his presidency in 2022, he is now on trial before the International Criminal Court in The Hague on charges arising from his bloody war on drugs. However, this does not mean that Southern authoritarian populism is a spent force in these countries: in Brazil, Bolsonaro’s son, Flavio, spearheaded the far-right movement that congealed around his father, and ran in the October 2026 presidential election, also losing to Lula. In the Philippines, the country’s new president, Bongbong Marcos, has mobilized the same authoritarian nostalgia – and many of the same political constituencies – that helped bring Duterte to power in 2016, while Duterte’s daughter, Sara Duterte, who is currently the country’s vice-president, is using her father’s enduring popularity with the Philippine electorate to make her own bid for the presidency in May 2028. 




Southern authoritarian populism in its emergent form is precisely that – emerging. It advances and retreats, develops new organizational forms, cultivates new leaders, and prepares for its next bid for power

.

 If the entrenched authoritarian populism of Erdogan and Modi shows us anything, it is what emergent authoritarian populism can become: durable regimes that transform democracies into electoral autocracies while deepening the neoliberal order and the precarity which it produces.




South Africa brings the argument full circle. Xenophobia has haunted the country’s democratic transition for nearly three decades. Since 2008, close to 700 people have been killed in xenophobic violence. But something new has happened in recent years. Xenophobic nationalism has become the organizing principle of an embryonic far-right ecosystem that stretches from the streets into party politics and, increasingly, the state. To understand why this has happened, we need to return to three themes: political economy, structures of feeling, and ideology.




South Africa’s post-apartheid political economy has produced exactly the kind of conjuncture I have been describing. More than three decades after the democratic transition, it remains the most unequal country in the world. The richest 10 per cent of the population receives two-thirds of all income and owns more than 85 per cent of all personal wealth. The bottom half receives just 5.6 per cent of national income and owns less than nothing: it lives in chronic debt. These inequalities remain profoundly racialized. Nearly three quarters of Black South Africans live below the country’s upper-bound poverty line, compared to little more than one per cent of White South Africans. At the same time, unemployment has become a permanent feature of everyday life, affecting more than four in ten people when discouraged work seekers are included.




These inequalities have persisted throughout the democratic era. Political liberation did not dismantle the structures of economic power inherited from colonialism and apartheid, and three decades of neoliberal restructuring have done little to change that reality. For many years, the ANC nevertheless retained popular consent through its liberation legacy and formidable organizational reach. But as poverty, unemployment, and inequality persisted, that hegemony gradually unravelled. Poor communities increasingly took to the streets to protest failing services, exclusion, and the absence of decent work. The ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time in 2024. South Africa, in other words, has entered precisely the kind of legitimation crisis that creates fertile ground for Southern authoritarian populism. 




Amid this overwhelming precarity, young Black South Africans are trying to build lives in conditions of chronic insecurity. Anxieties are rife in these efforts, but recent ethnographic work by South African anthropologist Hannah Dawson shows how life-making in Johannesburg’s townships is also animated by aspirations. The young township men at the centre want more than survival. They want the dignity, security, and material comforts that democratic citizenship seemed to promise. But when those aspirations collide with an economy that offers few stable opportunities, frustration searches for an object. That object is often the African migrants living alongside South Africans in the townships. They are blamed for driving down wages and worsening working conditions because they are seen as willing to take any job on offer. 




These popular resentments create an opening for xenophobic authoritarian populism to perform its ideological work. This is done by actors that extend from street movements such as Operation Dudula and March and March to political parties like the Patriotic Alliance, ActionSA, and, increasingly, Jacob Zuma’s MK Party. As the sociologist Jason Love argues, what binds these different actors together is a common ideological language. South Africa’s deep social crisis is attributed to the figure of the undocumented African migrant. This folk-devil is accused of stealing jobs, overwhelming public services, driving down wages, and bringing crime and drugs into South African communities. A crisis rooted in the country’s political economy becomes a crisis of illegal immigration. The political solution follows naturally: close the borders, deport the outsiders, and restore the nation to its rightful owners.




South Africa’s authoritarian populism remains embryonic. It has yet to construct a durable historic bloc and is still at some distance from capturing state power. But that does not make it politically insignificant. On the contrary, its ideological language is already reshaping South African politics. As xenophobic nationalism has gathered momentum, parties across the political spectrum have adopted tougher positions on immigration, while the Government of National Unity has tightened the country’s border regime. During the mobilizations of 2026, there were also unmistakable signs that the boundaries of the people-nation were beginning to shift again, as ethnonationalist appeals increasingly pitted Zulu South Africans against other Black communities. And all of this is unfolding at a time when growing numbers of South Africans – especially younger people – are turning away from electoral politics altogether. If faith in democratic participation continues to erode, the appeal of strongman leaders and authoritarian solutions may well grow stronger. South Africa, in other words, is no exception to the time of monsters that has descended on the Global South.




Understanding Southern authoritarian populism as a hegemonic project makes hope possible rather than despair convincing. The reason is simple.




When we understand Southern authoritarian populism as a hegemonic project – even in its most entrenched forms – what comes into view is not the overwhelming power of charismatic authoritarians who rule over populations that have succumbed to irrationality. Instead, we see a political project that has been painstakingly constructed through interventions into a specific conjuncture. And the hopeful thing about this is simple: anything that has been made can also be unmade.




The key thing that Southern authoritarian populism has made – or, in South Africa’s case, has begun to make – is historic blocs that bind elite interests and popular classes into revanchist people-nations. What the far right has articulated, democratic counterhegemonic projects must disarticulate. That work has to proceed along several interconnected fronts.




The first is political economy. Southern authoritarian populism has flourished where capitalist elites have appropriated a wildly disproportionate share of the wealth created by the working classes

.

 If the far right has built support on the ruins of zombie neoliberalism, then counterhegemonic alternatives cannot simply promise a kinder version of the same economic model. Instead, they must confront the class power of capital and build economies that guarantee security, dignity, and universal access to the public goods people need to live with dignity.




Radical structural reforms are therefore essential. But they cannot be conceived in purely material terms. They must go hand in hand with the work of disarticulating the people-nations that Southern authoritarian populism has built. Against the cruel optimism of believing that everyone can achieve individual prosperity through the marketplace, democratic counterhegemonic projects have to offer a different horizon: a vision of a community of life rooted in collective security, shared prosperity, and the expansion of human needs, capacities, and freedoms. In doing so, they must cultivate political subjectivities that reject majoritarianism, hierarchy, and exclusion, while forging new solidarities across the many lines of division that separate working people and subaltern groups. That is how new historic blocs are built.




Finally, counterhegemonic politics cannot be confined to the terrain of elections. If Southern authoritarian populism teaches us anything, it is that the most durable political victories are won long before ballots are cast. They are built patiently across the institutions and infrastructures of civil society – in neighbourhoods, workplaces, religious organizations, social movements, and digital spaces – before they are consolidated in the state. The tragic trajectory of too many popular uprisings in the Southern interregnum has been that once movements have demobilized, whether after winning concessions or toppling governments, reaction has regrouped and counterrevolution has followed. If Southern authoritarian populism is to be defeated, democratic counterhegemony must take root in ongoing popular struggles. It must be woven into the everyday work of organizing around the demands that have animated the great revolts of our time: bread, freedom, and social justice.
